retrieved_cards.title: A compared constant is the post-transform target, not the accepted input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: The accept check compares a constant (often in .rodata) against the input only after the input passes through a transform (arithmetic, bitwise, or encoding); the constant is the value the transformed input must equal.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A constant on the comparison path is read as the answer, but the comparison is against transform(input); the accepted input is the pre-image, not the constant.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Trace the transform on the input path and identify what must be inverted; then re-apply the transform to the recovered pre-image and check it reproduces the compared constant exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The visible constant is the flag and can be submitted directly.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: The constant is the post-transform comparison target; the accepted input is whatever transforms into it. Recover the pre-image before submitting.
not_applicable_when: the comparison is against the raw input with no transform on the path (then the constant may be the answer)
the constant is confirmed to be the operand compared against the raw input, with the transform applied elsewhere
the constant is used for output/formatting, not in the accept comparison
misfire_risks: may cause a constant to be dismissed even in trivial checks where the input is compared raw; confirm a transform is actually present before discarding the constant
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant is observed on the comparison path
a transform is observed between the input and the comparison

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract encode-then-compare pattern; no task-specific constants, transforms, or symbols.

retrieved_cards.title: XOR-then-compare: recover the input by XORing the target back
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A byte-wise XOR with a constant (single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent key) is applied to the input before it is compared against a constant byte sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: XOR is its own inverse; the compared bytes are input XOR key, so the visible target is the encoded form, not the input.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Read the key and whether it is single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent; XOR the target back; then XOR the recovered input forward again and check it reproduces the compared bytes exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The XORed/compared bytes are the flag, or the check is 'encrypted' and not worth pursuing.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: XOR the comparison target back with the same key to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no XOR appears on the comparison path
the XOR is applied to an unrelated buffer, not the input being checked
misfire_risks: the key may be position-dependent / rolling rather than a single constant byte; assuming a single-byte key yields a wrong pre-image -- verify the key schedule before inverting
minimum_evidence_before_use: an XOR operation is observed between the input and the comparison
the XOR operand (key) is identifiable or recoverable

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract XOR-then-compare; no task-specific keys, constants, or symbols.

retrieved_cards.title: Compared against a one-way digest: do NOT try to invert it
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: The input is compared against a fixed-length, high-entropy constant produced by a one-way function (hash/checksum); the transform is not reversible.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: Unlike invertible encodings, a digest cannot be reversed to the input; the visible digest is the comparison target, submitting it raw fails, and inverting it is also futile.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Identify the function as one-way; redirect effort to finding or constraining the pre-image rather than inverting; confirm a candidate by computing the digest of the candidate yourself and checking it equals the compared constant.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Submit the digest, or attempt to 'decrypt'/invert the hash to recover the input.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Recognize a one-way function: the accepted input must be found another way (located in the binary/inputs, or recovered by a constrained search), not by inverting the digest.
not_applicable_when: the transform is actually reversible (XOR/shift/encoding -- use the matching card and invert)
the constant is not a digest of the input
misfire_risks: mislabeling a reversible transform as one-way stops a valid inversion; distinguish a true digest (fixed length, avalanche) from an invertible encoding before abandoning inversion
minimum_evidence_before_use: the comparison target is a fixed-length high-entropy constant
the producing function matches a known one-way construction

retrieved_cards.mechanism: A statically-constant guard is overlooked, so a never-taken success branch is read as a live path to the flag.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the guard's value from the code (constant literal, build macro, or a global with no writer anywhere in the binary); a branch under a constant-false guard is dead and its contents are not evidence.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: This branch prints the flag / 'correct', so reaching it (or reading its contents) yields the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the guard: if it is constant-false via a literal or macro, the branch is dead and its contents do not gate acceptance.
not_applicable_when: the guard is a computed expression that only looks constant (that is decompiler_artifact / opaque-predicate, not this card)
the guard depends on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a guard that appears constant in one build may be configurable; confirm it in the disassembly, and check for writers to the global, rather than assuming from a source-like reconstruction
minimum_evidence_before_use: a success/flag branch is gated by a literal- or macro-constant condition

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract constant-guard dead-branch pattern; no task specifics. Distinct from opaque-predicate (computed) which is decompiler_artifact.

retrieved_cards.title: Compared against a one-way digest: do NOT try to invert it
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: The input is compared against a fixed-length, high-entropy constant produced by a one-way function (hash/checksum); the transform is not reversible.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: Unlike invertible encodings, a digest cannot be reversed to the input; the visible digest is the comparison target, submitting it raw fails, and inverting it is also futile.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Identify the function as one-way; redirect effort to finding or constraining the pre-image rather than inverting; confirm a candidate by computing the digest of the candidate yourself and checking it equals the compared constant.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Submit the digest, or attempt to 'decrypt'/invert the hash to recover the input.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Recognize a one-way function: the accepted input must be found another way (located in the binary/inputs, or recovered by a constrained search), not by inverting the digest.
not_applicable_when: the transform is actually reversible (XOR/shift/encoding -- use the matching card and invert)
the constant is not a digest of the input
misfire_risks: mislabeling a reversible transform as one-way stops a valid inversion; distinguish a true digest (fixed length, avalanche) from an invertible encoding before abandoning inversion
minimum_evidence_before_use: the comparison target is a fixed-length high-entropy constant
the producing function matches a known one-way construction

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract one-way-digest counter-case; no task-specific hashes or constants.

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

retrieved_cards.title: A success branch under a constant/macro guard is dead
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A branch that prints success or the flag is guarded by a condition that is constant at runtime via a literal or build macro (e.g. if(0), #ifdef DEBUG with DEBUG unset, a global never set true) -- readable as constant by inspection.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A statically-constant guard is overlooked, so a never-taken success branch is read as a live path to the flag.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the guard's value from the code (constant literal, build macro, or a global with no writer anywhere in the binary); a branch under a constant-false guard is dead and its contents are not evidence.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: This branch prints the flag / 'correct', so reaching it (or reading its contents) yields the answer.

minimum_evidence_before_use: a success/flag branch is gated by a literal- or macro-constant condition

retrieved_cards.title: Compared against a one-way digest: do NOT try to invert it
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: The input is compared against a fixed-length, high-entropy constant produced by a one-way function (hash/checksum); the transform is not reversible.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: Unlike invertible encodings, a digest cannot be reversed to the input; the visible digest is the comparison target, submitting it raw fails, and inverting it is also futile.

the constant is not a digest of the input

The VM executes based on a bytecode array at 0x404180. The dispatch reads bytecode[idx], computes bytecode[idx] % 19 to get opcode. If opcode == 18, it terminates. Otherwise it calls the function pointer at dispatch_table[opcode].

Function handlers (from addresses at 0x4040e0):
- 0x4011d6 (op 0): nop/load next bytecode value
- 0x40123a (op 1): exception throw / nop
- 0x401283 (op 2): add
- 0x4012dc (op 3): sub
- 0x401335 (op 4): imul
- 0x401396 (op 5): and
- 0x4013ef (op 7): xor

- 0x401700 (op 14): store to input array

- 0x401818 (op 17): nop

retrieved_cards.title: XOR-then-compare: recover the input by XORing the target back
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A byte-wise XOR with a constant (single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent key) is applied to the input before it is compared against a constant byte sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: XOR is its own inverse; the compared bytes are input XOR key, so the visible target is the encoded form, not the input.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Read the key and whether it is single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent; XOR the target back; then XOR the recovered input forward again and check it reproduces the compared bytes exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The XORed/compared bytes are the flag, or the check is 'encrypted' and not worth pursuing.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: XOR the comparison target back with the same key to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no XOR appears on the comparison path

minimum_evidence_before_use: an XOR operation is observed between the input and the comparison
the XOR operand (key) is identifiable or recoverable

retrieval_event.query:
The VM executes based on a bytecode array at 0x404180. The dispatch reads bytecode[idx], computes bytecode[idx] % 19 to get opcode. If opcode == 18, it terminates. Otherwise it calls the function pointer at dispatch_table[opcode].

Function handlers (from addresses at 0x4040e0):
- 0x4011d6 (op 0): nop/load next bytecode value
- 0x40123a (op 1): exception throw / nop
- 0x401283 (op 2): add
- 0x4012dc (op 3): sub
- 0x401335 (op 4): imul
- 0x401396 (op 5): and
- 0x4013ef (op 7): xor
- 0x401448 (op 8): or
- 0x4014a1 (op 8): shl
- 0x401509 (op 9): shr
- 0x401571 (op 10): mov (copy value)
- 0x4015ca (op 11): xchg
- 0x40162b (op 12): load from indirect
- 0x40169f (op 13): load from input array (0x63bb20)
- 0x401700 (op 14): store to input array
- 0x401761 (op 15): compare equal (sete)
- 0x4017cf (op 16): nop
- 0x401818 (op 17): nop

Catches exceptions and increments instruction pointer.

The key insight: when a handler throws an exception, it gets caught and the exception handler at 0x4018d7 adds rbx (which was set from the caught exception context - likely the "argument" from bytecode) to the instruction pointer 0x63bb08.

I need to trace the bytecode execution or use symbolic execution.

args.code:
# Let me read all the FDE entries to get the rbx values for each handler
import subprocess
result = subprocess.run(['readelf', '--debug-dump=frames', '{TARGET}'], 
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
# Parse the output to find all DW_CFA_val_expression for rbx
lines = result.stdout.split('\n')

print("Parsing FDE entries for rbx values:")
current_pc = None
for i, line in enumerate(lines):
    if 'FDE cie=' in line and 'pc=' in line:
        # Extract PC range
        import re
        match = re.search(r'pc=([0-9a-f]+)\.\.([0-9a-f]+)', line)
        if match:
            current_pc = (int(match.group(1), 16), int(match.group(2), 16))
            print(f"\nFDE: pc=0x{current_pc[0]:08x}..0x{current_pc[1]:08x}")
    if 'DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx)' in line:
        # Extract the constant value
        match = re.search(r'DW_OP_constu:\s*(\d+)', line)
        if match:
            rbx_val = int(match.group(1))
            print(f"  rbx = {rbx_val}")

retrieved_cards.title: A computed-constant branch is shown reachable but never executes
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Both arms of a branch are presented as reachable, but the controlling condition is a COMPUTED expression that is constant at runtime (an opaque predicate, e.g. an arithmetic identity), so one arm is in fact dead.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: The tool cannot evaluate a computed predicate, so it draws a branch as live; a constant-but-non-literal condition is then mistaken for a real decision point.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Write the condition out and settle it over its whole input domain -- a residue, parity or range argument often does it in one line, a solver does the rest; do not infer reachability from the tool's branch rendering.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Both branches can run, so the success/flag arm is reachable.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the predicate over the domain it operates on: if it is a computed constant, the corresponding arm is dead despite being drawn as reachable.
not_applicable_when: the controlling condition is a literal or build macro that is constant by inspection (that is dead_branch_constant_guard, not this card)
the predicate is confirmed to depend on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a predicate may be input-dependent and only look opaque; establish constancy by evaluating it rather than assuming any complex condition is opaque
minimum_evidence_before_use: a branch is drawn reachable under a non-literal computed condition
the condition's constancy is unconfirmed

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

retrieved_cards.title: A computed-constant branch is shown reachable but never executes
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Both arms of a branch are presented as reachable, but the controlling condition is a COMPUTED expression that is constant at runtime (an opaque predicate, e.g. an arithmetic identity), so one arm is in fact dead.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: The tool cannot evaluate a computed predicate, so it draws a branch as live; a constant-but-non-literal condition is then mistaken for a real decision point.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Write the condition out and settle it over its whole input domain -- a residue, parity or range argument often does it in one line, a solver does the rest; do not infer reachability from the tool's branch rendering.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Both branches can run, so the success/flag arm is reachable.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the predicate over the domain it operates on: if it is a computed constant, the corresponding arm is dead despite being drawn as reachable.
not_applicable_when: the controlling condition is a literal or build macro that is constant by inspection (that is dead_branch_constant_guard, not this card)
the predicate is confirmed to depend on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a predicate may be input-dependent and only look opaque; establish constancy by evaluating it rather than assuming any complex condition is opaque
minimum_evidence_before_use: a branch is drawn reachable under a non-literal computed condition
the condition's constancy is unconfirmed

retrieved_cards.title: A success branch under a constant/macro guard is dead
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A branch that prints success or the flag is guarded by a condition that is constant at runtime via a literal or build macro (e.g. if(0), #ifdef DEBUG with DEBUG unset, a global never set true) -- readable as constant by inspection.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A statically-constant guard is overlooked, so a never-taken success branch is read as a live path to the flag.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the guard's value from the code (constant literal, build macro, or a global with no writer anywhere in the binary); a branch under a constant-false guard is dead and its contents are not evidence.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: This branch prints the flag / 'correct', so reaching it (or reading its contents) yields the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the guard: if it is constant-false via a literal or macro, the branch is dead and its contents do not gate acceptance.
not_applicable_when: the guard is a computed expression that only looks constant (that is decompiler_artifact / opaque-predicate, not this card)
the guard depends on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a guard that appears constant in one build may be configurable; confirm it in the disassembly, and check for writers to the global, rather than assuming from a source-like reconstruction
minimum_evidence_before_use: a success/flag branch is gated by a literal- or macro-constant condition

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

retrieved_cards.title: A computed-constant branch is shown reachable but never executes
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Both arms of a branch are presented as reachable, but the controlling condition is a COMPUTED expression that is constant at runtime (an opaque predicate, e.g. an arithmetic identity), so one arm is in fact dead.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: The tool cannot evaluate a computed predicate, so it draws a branch as live; a constant-but-non-literal condition is then mistaken for a real decision point.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Write the condition out and settle it over its whole input domain -- a residue, parity or range argument often does it in one line, a solver does the rest; do not infer reachability from the tool's branch rendering.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Both branches can run, so the success/flag arm is reachable.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the predicate over the domain it operates on: if it is a computed constant, the corresponding arm is dead despite being drawn as reachable.
not_applicable_when: the controlling condition is a literal or build macro that is constant by inspection (that is dead_branch_constant_guard, not this card)
the predicate is confirmed to depend on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a predicate may be input-dependent and only look opaque; establish constancy by evaluating it rather than assuming any complex condition is opaque
minimum_evidence_before_use: a branch is drawn reachable under a non-literal computed condition
the condition's constancy is unconfirmed

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract opaque-predicate artifact; no task specifics. Distinct from dead_branch_constant_guard (literal/macro guard, readable).

retrieved_cards.title: A success branch under a constant/macro guard is dead
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A branch that prints success or the flag is guarded by a condition that is constant at runtime via a literal or build macro (e.g. if(0), #ifdef DEBUG with DEBUG unset, a global never set true) -- readable as constant by inspection.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A statically-constant guard is overlooked, so a never-taken success branch is read as a live path to the flag.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the guard's value from the code (constant literal, build macro, or a global with no writer anywhere in the binary); a branch under a constant-false guard is dead and its contents are not evidence.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: This branch prints the flag / 'correct', so reaching it (or reading its contents) yields the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the guard: if it is constant-false via a literal or macro, the branch is dead and its contents do not gate acceptance.
not_applicable_when: the guard is a computed expression that only looks constant (that is decompiler_artifact / opaque-predicate, not this card)
the guard depends on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a guard that appears constant in one build may be configurable; confirm it in the disassembly, and check for writers to the global, rather than assuming from a source-like reconstruction
minimum_evidence_before_use: a success/flag branch is gated by a literal- or macro-constant condition

- op 1 handler (0x40123a-0x401283): DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: 1)  -> rbx = 1
- op 2 handler (0x401283-0x4012dc): DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: 1)  -> rbx = 1
- op 3 handler (0x4012dc-0x401335): DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: 1)  -> rbx = 1
- op 4 handler (0x401335-0x401396): rbx = 1 (need to verify)

This means the instruction pointer increment is encoded in the unwind info!
- Op 0 (load) increments IP by 2 (to skip the argument)
- Other ops increment IP by 1

This explains the control flow. Now I can properly trace the VM execution.

# Let me search for the FDE entries for ops 16 and 17 more carefully
import subprocess
result = subprocess.run(['readelf', '--debug-dump=frames', '{TARGET}'], 
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
text = result.stdout

# Search for FDE entries around 0x4017cf and 0x401818
import re

# Find all FDE entries
fde_pattern = r'FDE cie=\w+ pc=([0-9a-f]+)\.\.([0-9a-f]+)'
matches = re.findall(fde_pattern, text)
print("All FDE entries:")
for start, end in matches:
    s = int(start, 16)
    e = int(end, 16)
    print(f"  0x{s:08x}..0x{e:08x}")

# Find rbx val_expression patterns
val_expr_pattern = r'FDE.*?pc=([0-9a-f]+)\.\.([0-9a-f]+).*?(?:DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 \(rbx\) \(DW_OP_constu: (\d+)\))?'

# Parse FDE blocks
fde_blocks = text.split('FDE cie=')[1:]  # Skip header
print("\n\nFDE blocks with rbx values:")
for block in fde_blocks:
    pc_match = re.search(r'pc=([0-9a-f]+)\.\.([0-9a-f]+)', block)
    rbx_match = re.search(r'DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 \(rbx\) \(DW_OP_constu: (\d+)\)', block)
    if pc_match:
        s, e = int(pc_match.group(1), 16), int(pc_match.group(2), 16)
        rbx_val = int(rbx_match.group(1)) if rbx_match else 'NOT SET'
        print(f"  0x{s:08x}..0x{e:08x}: rbx = {rbx_val}")

- op 1 handler (0x40123a-0x401283): DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: 1)  -> rbx = 1
- op 2 handler (0x401283-0x4012dc): DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: 1)  -> rbx = 1
- op 3 handler (0x4012dc-0x401335): DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: 1)  -> rbx = 1

# But here's the key insight: when these handlers throw, the exception is caught
# by the VM dispatcher's catch block, and then rbx is added to IP

# If rbx is NOT SET via val_expression, the personality function restores rbx
# from the caller's saved register frame. But what value is that?

# Looking at the VM dispatcher (0x401861):
# push rbp
# push rbx  <- saves whatever rbx was when dispatcher was called
# sub rsp, 8
# ... loop ...

# The dispatcher's rbx comes from the main function's call
# But before that, what is rbx in main?

# Actually, let me check more carefully - maybe the handlers DO have a different
# mechanism for setting rbx

# Op 17 without rbx being set means rbx = whatever caller had
# In the VM dispatcher, after the first op is executed, rbx might be set by 
# the first handler's unwinding, and subsequent ops might use that value!

# Let me trace more carefully with this understanding:
# - Op 0 sets rbx = 2 during unwinding
# - After op 0, the catch block adds 2 to IP
# - Then the next op executes
# - If the next op also sets rbx during unwinding, that value is used
# - If the next op DOESN'T set rbx (like op 16/17), the previous rbx value persists!

# But wait, that's not quite right either because:
# - After catching, the code jumps back to the loop
# - rbx is on the stack (pushed at dispatcher entry)
# - When the next handler is called, it pushes its own registers
# - During unwinding from the handler, rbx might be set OR restored

# If there's no val_expression, rbx is restored from saved value
# But what's the saved value? It's from where the exception was thrown.

# push r12, push rbp, push rbx (saves the dispatcher's rbx)
# ... do stuff, set rbx = exception_object
# throw exception
# During unwinding: if val_expression, rbx = constant; else rbx = saved value

# But wait, the saved value is from the handler's stack (the push rbx at entry)
# which is the dispatcher's rbx

# And the dispatcher's rbx came from... the main function's call

# Let me check what main sets rbx to before calling the dispatcher

# The VM loop at 0x40186e processes bytecode until opcode == 18
# Each handler throws, and the catch adds rbx to IP

# If op 16/17 doesn't set rbx, and the saved rbx is some large value,
# the IP might jump to a completely different location!

# Let me check bytecode[11] which was loaded in step 6:
# bytecode[11] = 0x000000000002fac1 
# This is loaded as arg1

# Then step 7 is op 17 at IP=12
# If rbx is NOT set, what happens?

# Actually, I think the solution might be simpler
# Let me check if the bytecode value itself encodes the IP increment differently
# for ops 16 and 17

import struct

with open("{TARGET}", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()

def addr_to_offset(addr):
    return addr - 0x404060 + 0x3060

bytecode_offset = addr_to_offset(0x404180)

# Check bytecode entries with opcode 16 or 17
print("Bytecode entries with opcode 16 or 17:")
for i in range(200):
    offset = bytecode_offset + i*8
    if offset + 8 > len(data):
        break
    val = struct.unpack('<Q', data[offset:offset+8])[0]
    opcode = val % 19
    if opcode in [16, 17]:
        # The upper bits might encode something
        upper = val >> 8
        print(f"  [{i}] val=0x{val:016x}, opcode={opcode}, val//19={val//19}")

retrieved_cards.mechanism: The tool cannot evaluate a computed predicate, so it draws a branch as live; a constant-but-non-literal condition is then mistaken for a real decision point.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Write the condition out and settle it over its whole input domain -- a residue, parity or range argument often does it in one line, a solver does the rest; do not infer reachability from the tool's branch rendering.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Both branches can run, so the success/flag arm is reachable.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the predicate over the domain it operates on: if it is a computed constant, the corresponding arm is dead despite being drawn as reachable.
not_applicable_when: the controlling condition is a literal or build macro that is constant by inspection (that is dead_branch_constant_guard, not this card)
the predicate is confirmed to depend on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a predicate may be input-dependent and only look opaque; establish constancy by evaluating it rather than assuming any complex condition is opaque
minimum_evidence_before_use: a branch is drawn reachable under a non-literal computed condition
the condition's constancy is unconfirmed

retrieved_cards.title: A success branch under a constant/macro guard is dead
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A branch that prints success or the flag is guarded by a condition that is constant at runtime via a literal or build macro (e.g. if(0), #ifdef DEBUG with DEBUG unset, a global never set true) -- readable as constant by inspection.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A statically-constant guard is overlooked, so a never-taken success branch is read as a live path to the flag.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the guard's value from the code (constant literal, build macro, or a global with no writer anywhere in the binary); a branch under a constant-false guard is dead and its contents are not evidence.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: This branch prints the flag / 'correct', so reaching it (or reading its contents) yields the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the guard: if it is constant-false via a literal or macro, the branch is dead and its contents do not gate acceptance.
not_applicable_when: the guard is a computed expression that only looks constant (that is decompiler_artifact / opaque-predicate, not this card)
the guard depends on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a guard that appears constant in one build may be configurable; confirm it in the disassembly, and check for writers to the global, rather than assuming from a source-like reconstruction
minimum_evidence_before_use: a success/flag branch is gated by a literal- or macro-constant condition

retrieval_event.query:
CRITICAL DISCOVERY: The .eh_frame section contains DW_CFA_val_expression directives that SET rbx during exception unwinding!

For each handler:
- op 0 handler (0x4011d6-0x40123a): DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: 2)  -> rbx = 2
- op 1 handler (0x40123a-0x401283): DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: 1)  -> rbx = 1
- op 2 handler (0x401283-0x4012dc): DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: 1)  -> rbx = 1
- op 3 handler (0x4012dc-0x401335): DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_constu: 1)  -> rbx = 1
- op 4 handler (0x401335-0x401396): rbx = 1 (need to verify)

This means the instruction pointer increment is encoded in the unwind info!
- Op 0 (load) increments IP by 2 (to skip the argument)
- Other ops increment IP by 1

This explains the control flow. Now I can properly trace the VM execution.

args.text:
CRITICAL DISCOVERY - The VM uses DWARF expressions in eh_frame to control execution!

For op 16 (handler 0x4017cf):
- DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_breg7 (rsp): -4080; DW_OP_deref)
- This means: rbx = *(rsp - 4080) = *(rsp - 0xff0)
- rsp-0xff0 is where arg1 is stored! So rbx = arg1

For op 17 (handler 0x401818):
- DW_CFA_val_expression: r3 (rbx) (DW_OP_breg7 (rsp): -4064; DW_OP_deref; DW_OP_constu: 0; DW_OP_eq; DW_OP_bra: 7; DW_OP_breg7 (rsp): -4080; DW_OP_deref; DW_OP_skip: 1; DW_OP_lit1)
- This is a conditional: if *(rsp-4064) == 0 then rbx = *(rsp-4080) else rbx = 1
- rsp-4064 is rsp-0xfe0 which is arg2 (result)
- So: if arg2 == 0, rbx = arg1, else rbx = 1

This means:
- Op 16: unconditional jump by arg1 (IP += arg1)
- Op 17: conditional jump: if arg2 == 0, IP += arg1, else IP += 1

The VM now makes sense! Op 16/17 are control flow instructions!

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

args.code:
# Now I can properly trace the VM execution!
# Op meanings:
# op 0: load arg from bytecode[ip+1] into arg1, IP += 2
# op 1: nop, IP += 1
# op 2: arg2 += arg1, IP += 1
# op 3: arg2 -= arg1, IP += 1
# op 4: arg2 *= arg1, IP += 1
# op 5: arg2 &= arg1, IP += 1
# op 6: arg2 |= arg1, IP += 1
# op 7: arg2 ^= arg1, IP += 1
# op 8: arg2 <<= (arg1 & 0x3f), IP += 1
# op 9: arg2 >>= (arg1 & 0x3f), IP += 1
# op 10: copy arg1 to some location, IP += 1
# op 11: xchg arg1, arg2, IP += 1
# op 12: indirect load from stack, IP += 2
# op 13: load input[arg1] to arg1, IP += 1
# op 14: store arg2 to input[arg1], IP += 1
# op 15: arg2 = (arg2 == arg1) ? 1 : 0, IP += 1
# op 16: IP += arg1 (unconditional jump)
# op 17: if arg2 == 0: IP += arg1 else IP += 1 (conditional jump)
# op 18: EXIT

import struct

with open("{TARGET}", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()

def addr_to_offset(addr):
    return addr - 0x404060 + 0x3060

bytecode_offset = addr_to_offset(0x404180)

def get_bytecode(ip):
    offset = bytecode_offset + ip * 8
    return struct.unpack('<Q', data[offset:offset+8])[0]

# Simulate the VM
# State: IP, arg1 (stack -0xff0), arg2 (stack -0xfe0), input[8]
ip = 0
arg1 = 0  # rsp - 0xff0
arg2 = 0  # rsp - 0xfe0
# Use symbolic input for now
input_arr = [f'input[{i}]' for i in range(8)]

max_steps = 500
step = 0
trace = []

print("--- VM Execution Trace ---")
while step < max_steps:
    bc = get_bytecode(ip)
    opcode = bc % 19
    
    if opcode == 18:
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={ip:3d}: EXIT")
        break
    
    old_ip = ip
    old_arg1 = arg1
    old_arg2 = arg2
    
    if opcode == 0:  # LOAD
        arg = get_bytecode(ip + 1)
        arg1 = arg
        ip += 2
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: LOAD arg1 = 0x{arg:016x}")
    elif opcode == 1:  # NOP
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: NOP")
    elif opcode == 2:  # ADD
        if isinstance(arg2, str) or isinstance(arg1, str):
            arg2 = f"({arg2} + {hex(arg1) if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1})"
        else:
            arg2 = (arg2 + arg1) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: ADD arg2 += arg1")
    elif opcode == 3:  # SUB
        if isinstance(arg2, str) or isinstance(arg1, str):
            arg2 = f"({arg2} - {hex(arg1) if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1})"
        else:
            arg2 = (arg2 - arg1) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: SUB arg2 -= arg1")
    elif opcode == 4:  # MUL
        if isinstance(arg2, str) or isinstance(arg1, str):
            arg2 = f"({arg2} * {hex(arg1) if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1})"
        else:
            arg2 = (arg2 * arg1) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: MUL arg2 *= arg1")
    elif opcode == 5:  # AND
        if isinstance(arg2, str) or isinstance(arg1, str):
            arg2 = f"({arg2} & {hex(arg1) if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1})"
        else:
            arg2 = arg2 & arg1
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: AND arg2 &= arg1")
    elif opcode == 6:  # OR
        if isinstance(arg2, str) or isinstance(arg1, str):
            arg2 = f"({arg2} | {hex(arg1) if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1})"
        else:
            arg2 = arg2 | arg1
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: OR arg2 |= arg1")
    elif opcode == 7:  # XOR
        if isinstance(arg2, str) or isinstance(arg1, str):
            arg2 = f"({arg2} ^ {hex(arg1) if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1})"
        else:
            arg2 = arg2 ^ arg1
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: XOR arg2 ^= arg1")
    elif opcode == 8:  # SHL
        shift = arg1 & 0x3f if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1
        if isinstance(arg2, str):
            arg2 = f"({arg2} << {shift})"
        else:
            arg2 = (arg2 << shift) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: SHL arg2 <<= (arg1 & 0x3f)")
    elif opcode == 9:  # SHR
        shift = arg1 & 0x3f if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1
        if isinstance(arg2, str):
            arg2 = f"({arg2} >> {shift})"
        else:
            arg2 = arg2 >> shift
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: SHR arg2 >>= (arg1 & 0x3f)")
    elif opcode == 10:  # MOV (copy to temp)
        # This seems to copy arg1 to a temp location
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: MOV (temp = arg1)")
    elif opcode == 11:  # XCHG
        arg1, arg2 = arg2, arg1
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: XCHG arg1, arg2")
    elif opcode == 12:  # ILOAD (indirect load from stack)
        arg = get_bytecode(ip + 1)
        # This loads from a computed stack address
        ip += 2
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: ILOAD (indirect) with arg=0x{arg:016x}")
    elif opcode == 13:  # LOAD_INPUT
        idx = arg1 & 7 if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1
        if isinstance(idx, int):
            arg1 = input_arr[idx]
        else:
            arg1 = f"input[{idx}]"
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: LOAD_INPUT arg1 = input[{idx}]")
    elif opcode == 14:  # STORE_INPUT
        idx = arg1 & 7 if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1
        if isinstance(idx, int):
            input_arr[idx] = arg2
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: STORE_INPUT input[{idx}] = arg2")
    elif opcode == 15:  # CMP_EQ
        if isinstance(arg1, int) and isinstance(arg2, int):
            arg2 = 1 if arg2 == arg1 else 0
        else:
            arg2 = f"({arg2} == {hex(arg1) if isinstance(arg1, int) else arg1})"
        ip += 1
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: CMP_EQ arg2 = (arg2 == arg1)")
    elif opcode == 16:  # JMP (unconditional)
        jump = arg1 if isinstance(arg1, int) else 0
        ip += jump
        print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: JMP by {jump} -> IP={ip}")
    elif opcode == 17:  # JMP_IF_ZERO (conditional)
        if isinstance(arg2, int):
            if arg2 == 0:
                jump = arg1 if isinstance(arg1, int) else 0
                ip += jump
                print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: JZ (arg2==0) -> JMP by {jump} -> IP={ip}")
            else:
                ip += 1
                print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: JZ (arg2!=0) -> IP={ip}")
        else:
            # Symbolic - need to explore both branches
            print(f"[{step:3d}] IP={old_ip:3d}: JZ (symbolic arg2={arg2})")
            ip += 1  # Assume not zero for now
    
    trace.append((old_ip, opcode, arg1, arg2))
    step += 1
    
    if step > 100:
        print(f"... truncated at step {step}")
        break

print(f"\nTotal steps: {step}")
print(f"\nFinal input array state:")
for i, val in enumerate(input_arr):
    print(f"  input[{i}] = {val}")

retrieved_cards.title: Disassembly can desync and show a plausible-but-wrong instruction stream
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Instructions are being read at a fixed alignment where the real code overlaps, jumps into the middle of an instruction, or uses anti-disassembly, so the decoded stream may not be what executes.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A byte stream has multiple decodings; a linear or fixed-offset decode can lock onto the wrong one, producing instructions that look real but are not executed as shown.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Follow control flow into the region to fix the instruction boundaries, and re-disassemble at that alignment; where two decodings are possible, the one an incoming edge lands on is the one that runs.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The disassembly listing is the executed code, so I can reverse it as-is.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Verify the decode alignment against control flow; re-disassemble from the real entry points and follow the jumps to recover the instructions that actually run.
not_applicable_when: the disassembly alignment is confirmed by an incoming control-flow edge
the code region is known-clean with no overlap/anti-disasm
misfire_risks: most disassembly is correctly aligned; suspect desync specifically around indirect jumps, inline data, or obfuscated regions, not everywhere
minimum_evidence_before_use: a region shows overlap / jump-into-instruction / anti-disassembly characteristics
its alignment has not been confirmed against an incoming control-flow edge

retrieved_cards.title: Code after an unconditional transfer is unreachable
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A flag print or 'correct' path sits after an unconditional control transfer (return, exit, or unconditional jump) in the same flow, making it physically unreachable.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: Linear reading of code overlooks that a prior unconditional transfer prevents the later success path from executing.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Enumerate the incoming edges of the block; code dominated by an unconditional return/exit/jump with no other incoming edge does not execute.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The later success/flag code runs, so it determines acceptance.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Trace control flow: code dominated by a prior unconditional return/exit/jump does not execute and cannot gate acceptance.
not_applicable_when: control flow can actually reach the path (e.g. via another edge)
the transfer is conditional, not unconditional
misfire_risks: a path may be reachable via an edge not obvious in a linear view; enumerate incoming edges (jump tables, indirect targets, exception paths) before concluding unreachability
minimum_evidence_before_use: a success path sits after an unconditional transfer on the same flow
